newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Socialists defend conditions for euro.
newsitem.headline: France's Socialists defend conditions for euro.

text.p: The leader of France's Socialists, Lionel Jospin, defended his conditions for a European single currency on Sunday, including a call for Spain and Italy to be in from the start.

Speaking a week before the first round of snap parliamentary elections, he said he did not expect the issue to cause a split with conservative President Jacques Chirac if the left won control of the National Assembly, which it lost in 1993.
"What I see is that everyone is coming round to the conditions which the Socialists have placed on the transition to a single currency," he told France 3 television.

He mentioned the views of outgoing National Assembly (lower house) speaker Philippe Seguin, who called on Europe's leaders earlier to repair an "intolerable" gap on employment in the preparations for a single currency to be launched in 1999.

The Socialists support monetary union but on certain conditions. Spain and Italy should be among the first to join, the new euro currency should not be overvalued against the dollar, a European economic government should counterbalance the European central bank and euro zone countries should be bound by a growth and solidarity pact to promote jobs.
"These conditions should not pose problems for France because they are in France's interests and also, in my view, in the euro's interests and those of Europe," Jospin said.
He said Germany's decision last week to revalue gold reserves to help prepare the launch had reinforced his view.

"It is not an area in which I can imagine real difficulties betweeen us and the current president," he said, referring to the prospect of power-sharing with Chirac if the left wins the two-round election Chirac has called for May 25 and June 1.
He added his opposition to an overvalued euro against the dollar did not mean the shared currency should be "weak."
Latest opinion polls suggest Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right coalition will defeat the Socialists and stay in government, but with a reduced number of seats.

Juppe's predecessor, former conservative prime minister Edouard Balladur, said earlier he hoped Spain, Italy and Portugal would be among the first to join the euro but it was wrong for Jospin's Socialists to make this a condition.

"I hope with all my heart that Italy, Spain and Portugal will be in (the single currency) but to say that if they cannot, then we won't do monetary union, is against the (Maastricht) treaty and the interests of France," he told the Journal du Dimanche newspaper in an interview.
